summary: An IAB essay on the end-to-end principle, the core design guideline of the Internet. It traces how the principle has been applied over time and considers how trends such as middleboxes in the network affect it. It then draws conclusions about how the principle and the architecture should evolve.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3724 is an Internet Architecture Board essay about the end-to-end principle, the rule that says a network should only do what cannot be done correctly at the ends of a connection. The authors look at how the rule has been stretched since 1984, at the three forces pushing back against it, and at what the principle should mean now that networks carry services and users do not trust each other.

questions: why do middleboxes break end to end
why do middleboxes threaten the end-to-end principle
subtitle: An IAB essay on the Internet's core design rule, and on the pressure put on it by middleboxes and trust

tldr.problem: The end-to-end principle says that a function should live in the end points unless it can be done correctly only there, but the Internet of 2004 is full of network operators, firewalls and services that want to act in the middle.
tldr.mechanism: The memo traces how the principle grew from a narrow argument about delivery guarantees into a general rule about where state should live, then examines the trends pushing against it: the loss of trust between users, services that promise a performance level, and the rise of commercial intermediaries.
tldr.outcome: Rather than defend the principle as a fundamentalism, the authors argue it should be rebuilt around its two purposes, protecting innovation and providing reliability and trust, and that every proposal to put services in the network should be weighed against user choice, integrity, trust and innovation.

today: RFC 3724 is an Informational memo from March 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an Internet Architecture Board essay rather than a specification, and it proposes no protocols, so it raises no new security considerations of its own.

sections.title: What This Memo Does
sections.content:
One of the key architectural guidelines of the Internet is the end-to-end principle in the papers by Saltzer, Reed and Clark. It was originally articulated as a question of where best not to put functions in a communication system. Over the ensuing years it evolved to address concerns of maintaining openness, increasing reliability and robustness, and preserving the properties of user choice and ease of new service development, as discussed by Blumenthal and Clark, and those concerns were not part of the original articulation.

This document examines how the interpretation of the principle has evolved over the years and where it stands currently. It examines trends in the development of the Internet that have led to pressure to define services in the network, a topic that has already received attention from the IAB in RFC 3238, and describes some considerations about how the principle might evolve in light of those trends.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is an essay, not a specification. It asks how the Internet's founding rule should be applied to a network that now carries services, sits behind firewalls and connects people who do not trust each other.

sections.title: How the Principle Evolved
sections.content:
In the beginning, the principle was a statement about where a function can be implemented correctly. The wording is that the function in question can be completely and correctly implemented only with the knowledge and help of the application standing at the end points, so providing it as a feature of the communication system itself is not possible, though an incomplete version may sometimes be useful as a performance enhancement.

Delivery guarantees were the example. The original ARPANET returned a message, Request for Next Message, whenever it delivered a packet. The message was useful inside the network as a form of congestion control, since the ARPANET refused to accept another message to the same destination until the previous acknowledgement was returned, but it was never particularly useful as an indication of guaranteed delivery. The problem was that the sending host does not want to know only that the network delivered a packet, but that the receiving host's stack properly processed it. In terms of the modern IP stack, a reliable transport layer needs an indication that transport processing completed, such as TCP's ACK message, and not simply an indication from the IP layer that the packet arrived. The examples given at the time primarily involved transmission of data packets: data integrity, delivery guarantees, duplicate message suppression, per packet encryption and transaction management.

In the middle, the principle widened to a question of where best to put the state associated with applications, in the network or at the end nodes. RFC 1958 states that an end-to-end protocol design should not rely on the maintenance of state inside the network, that such state should be maintained only in the endpoints, in such a way that it can only be destroyed when the endpoint itself breaks, known as fate-sharing, and that everything else should be done at the fringes. RFC 1958 uses the term application to mean the entire network stack on the end node, and the fate of a conversation between two applications is shared only between the two applications; the fate does not depend on anything in the network, except the network's ability to get packets from one application to the other.

What the network maintains is soft state: routes, the QoS guarantees it makes, session information used in header compression, compression histories, and the like. That state must be self-healing, adaptive procedures must exist to derive and maintain it, its volume must be minimised, and the loss of it must not cause more than a temporary denial of service given that connectivity exists. Manually configured state must be kept to an absolute minimum. Hard state, on which the proper functioning of the application depends, is maintained only in the end nodes.

And now, the memo offers an example of the principle still influencing debate, in IP mobility. The existing routing architecture severely constrains how closely IP mobility can match the principle. Mobile IPv6 requires a routing proxy in the mobile node's home network, the Home Agent, to maintain the mapping between the mobile node's routing locator, the care of address, and its node identifier, the home address. But the local subnet routing proxy, the Foreign Agent, which was a feature of the older Mobile IPv4 design that compromised end-to-end routing, has been eliminated, and the end node now handles its own care of address. Mobile IPv6 also includes secure mechanisms for optimising routing to allow end-to-end routing between the mobile end node and the correspondent node. The remaining need for the Home Agent is determined by the aliasing of the global node identifier with the routing identifier in the Internet routing architecture, a topic reported in RFC 2956 that has not changed in IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The principle started narrow: only the ends can know whether a file arrived intact. It then grew into a rule about where state lives, so that the network keeps only soft state that can rebuild itself. Mobile IP shows the same logic: the end node now looks after its own care-of address, and the only thing left in the middle is what the routing system forces.

sections.title: Trends Running Against the Principle
sections.content:
The specific application of the end-to-end principle described in RFC 1958 has increasingly come into question from various directions, and the IAB has been concerned about this for some time, for example in RFC 2956 and RFC 2775. The primary focus of those documents is the reduction in transparency due to the introduction of NATs and other address translation mechanisms, and the consequences of scenarios involving full, partial or no deployment of IPv6. More recently the topic of concern has shifted to the consequences of service deployment in the network. The IAB opinion on Open Pluggable Edge Services in RFC 3238 is intended to assess the architectural desirability of defining services in the network and to raise questions about how such services might compromise privacy, security and end-to-end data integrity.

The first trend is the need for authentication. Perhaps the single most important change from the Internet of 15 years ago is the lack of trust between users. The end users of the Internet of 15 years ago were few and largely dedicated to academic research, and trust between end users and between network operators and their users was simply not an issue. Today the motivations of some individuals are not always entirely ethical, and even when they are, the assumption that end nodes will always co-operate to achieve a mutually beneficial action is not always accurate. The growth in users who are either not technologically sophisticated enough or simply uninterested in maintaining their own security has required network operators to become more proactive in deploying measures to prevent naive or uninterested users from generating security problems.

The end-to-end principle does not require users to trust each other, but the lack of trust requires application and system designers to make a choice about how to handle authentication. The most common network elements interposed between end hosts are those dedicated to security: firewalls, VPN tunnel endpoints and certificate servers. These intermediaries are designed to protect the network from attack, or to allow two end nodes whose users have no inherent reason to trust each other to achieve some level of authentication. At the same time, these measures act as impediments to end-to-end communication. Third party trust intermediaries are not a requirement for security, since end-to-end mechanisms such as S/MIME can be used instead, and where third party measures such as PKI infrastructure or keys in DNS are used to exchange keying material they do not necessarily impinge on end-to-end traffic once authentication has been achieved. Even if third parties are involved, it is up to the endpoints and their users to determine which third parties they trust.

The second trend is new service models. New services inspired by new applications require achieving the proper performance level as a fundamental part of the delivered service, which is a significant change from the original best effort model. Email, file transfer and even Web access are not perceived as failing if performance degrades, though the user may be frustrated at the time required. For streaming audio and video, and for real time bidirectional voice and video, achieving the proper performance level is part of delivering the service, and a customer contracting for the service has a right to expect the level of performance they paid for. Content distributors sometimes release content through distribution servers spread around the Internet to avoid delays when the server is topologically far from the client, and retail broadband and multimedia services are a new service model for many providers.

The third trend is the rise of the third party. Academic and government institutions ran the Internet of 15 years ago and did not expect to make a profit, whereas the network operator most users deal with today is the commercial ISP, whose investors expect a profit. The retail dialup bit pipe with email and shell access has become a commodity service with low profit margins, so some operators want to deploy service models with higher profit potential. An example is retail broadband access via cable or DSL coupled with streaming multimedia. Some ISPs also deploy content distribution networks to improve the performance of streaming media, typically deployed so that they are only accessible within the ISP's own network, so they do not contribute to open, end-to-end service. Corporate network administrators and governmental officials have become increasingly demanding of opportunities to interpose between two parties in an end-to-end conversation. A benign motivation is to mitigate the lack of trust, so the third party acts as a trust anchor or enforcer of good behaviour between the two ends. A less benign motivation is for the third party to insert policy for its own reasons, perhaps taxation or even censorship. The requirements of third parties often derive from social and legal considerations rather than technical ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things have changed since the 1980s: people no longer assume strangers are honest, some services now promise a quality level as part of the deal, and commercial operators want to sit in the middle of other people's conversations. Each pushes the network towards doing things the ends used to do.

sections.title: Whither the End-to-End Principle
sections.content:
Given the pressures on the principle, a question arises about its future: does it have a future in the Internet architecture, and if so, how should it be applied? The authors argue that an unproductive approach is to insist on the principle as a fundamentalist principle that allows no compromise. The pressures described are real and powerful, and if the technical community ignores them, the likely result is a market opportunity for a new technical community that does not ignore them but which may not understand the implications of its design choices. A more productive approach is to return to first principles and re-examine what the principle is trying to accomplish, and then update the definition and exposition of the principle given the complexities of the Internet today.

The two primary desirable consequences of the principle are the protection of innovation and the provision of reliability and robustness. Protection of innovation follows because requiring modification in the network to deploy a new service is still typically more difficult than modifying end nodes. The counterargument, that many end nodes are closed boxes and most users do not want to update them anyway, does not apply to all nodes and all users: many end nodes are still user configurable, and a sizable percentage of users are early adopters willing to put up with some technological grief to try out a new idea. Requiring someone with a new idea to convince a bunch of ISPs or corporate administrators to modify their networks is much more difficult than putting up a web page with some downloadable software implementing the service.

Reliability and trust are of increasing concern, because of the decrease in reliability and robustness that results from deliberate, active attacks on the network infrastructure and end nodes. The original developers were concerned with large-scale system failures, but attacks of the subtlety and variety the Internet experiences today were not a problem during the original development. The end-to-end principle was not addressed to that decrease, so the trust breakdown is another forcing function on the Internet architecture.

The reaction to the trust breakdown has been to back-fit security into existing protocols. The authors argue that this is necessary but not sufficient, and that the issue of trust must become as firm an architectural principle in protocol design as the end-to-end principle is today. Trust is not simply a matter of adding cryptographic protection to a protocol after it is designed. Before designing the protocol, the trust relationships between the network elements involved must be defined, and boundaries drawn between those elements that share a trust relationship. Those trust boundaries should determine what type of communication occurs between network elements and which elements signal each other, and when communication crosses a trust boundary some form of cryptographic or other security protection may be necessary. Additional measures may be needed when communicating elements do not share a trust relationship, for example a protocol might need to minimise state in the recipient before establishing the validity of the sender's credentials, to avoid a memory depletion denial of service attack.

The concern expressed by the principle applies to application design too. Two key points are to ensure application protocols have no dependencies that would break the end-to-end principle, such as layer violations, and that they can identify end points in a consistent fashion. The desire to insert more application infrastructure into the network need not violate the principle if the partitioning of function is done so that services provided in the network operate with the explicit knowledge and involvement of endpoints, where that is necessary for the proper functioning of the service. The result becomes a distributed application, in which the principle applies to each connection involved in implementing it.

Internet standards have increasingly become an arena for conflict. ISPs have certain concerns, businesses and government have others, and vendors of networking hardware and software still others, and sometimes these conflict with the concerns of end users. ISPs are reluctant to deploy interdomain quality of service services because every known instance creates a significant and easily exploited denial of service vulnerability, while some end users would like end-to-end, Diffserv or Intserv-style QoS available to improve support for voice and video between end nodes in different domains. Some of these conflicts are impossible to resolve on a technical level and would not even be desirable, because they involve social and legal choices the IETF is not empowered to make. For those conflicts that do involve technical choices, the important properties of user choice and empowerment, reliability and integrity of end-to-end service, supporting trust and good network citizen behaviour, and fostering innovation in services should be the basis on which resolution is made.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors do not want the principle treated as a religion. They want it rebuilt around what it was for: letting new services be built without asking anyone's permission, and keeping the network trustworthy. They also want trust itself to be a design rule, drawn as a boundary before the protocol is written, not bolted on afterwards.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
The end-to-end principle continues to guide technical development of Internet standards, and remains as important today for the Internet architecture as in the past. In many cases, unbundling the principle into its consequences leads to a distributed approach in which the principle applies to interactions between the individual pieces of an application, while the unbundled consequences, protection of innovation, reliability and robustness, apply to the entire application.

While the principle originated as a focused argument about the need for the knowledge and assistance of end nodes to properly implement functions, particular second order properties developed by the Internet as a result of it have come to be recognised as being as important, if not more so, than the principle itself. End user choice and empowerment, integrity of service, support for trust and good network citizen behaviour are all properties that developed as a consequence of the end-to-end principle. Recognising these properties in a particular proposal for modifications to the Internet has become more important than before as the pressures to incorporate services into the network have increased, and any proposal to incorporate services in the network should be weighed against these properties before proceeding.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is still worth keeping, but it is now judged by what it produced: choice for users, services that keep working, trust between strangers, and room to invent. Any new service in the network should be measured against those before it is built.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that it does not propose any new protocols, and therefore does not involve any security considerations in that sense. However, throughout the document there are discussions of privacy and integrity issues and the architectural requirements created by those issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes any protocol, so there is nothing new to secure. The privacy and integrity arguments are made in the body of the essay instead.
